title: digest drops a valid cut when an identical break from a partly single-stranded site sorts first (sticky input ends)
expected: Each digest yields 2 fragments: EcoRI (and MlyI, BsmAI) cut at a fully double-stranded site whose cut zone lies inside the duplex. Adding a second enzyme never removes a valid cut. A skipped event names the site that could not cut.
actual: Each digest yields 1 fragment (the molecule is not cut). For EcoRI+BsmBI, `skipped` is [["BsmBI","end","BsmBI (site at 17) cannot cut: its recognition site is not fully double-stranded"]]; EcoRI's event is neither applied nor reported. For MlyI and BsaI+BsmAI, only the partly single-stranded site at position 1 is reported as skipped. In 6,000 fuzzed sticky-end digests against an independent reference, 7 disagreed, all with this root cause.

title: Conflict tie-break contradicts the documented rule: zone ties are broken by `top`, not by enzyme name
description:
The digest.ts header documents the conflict rule: "the first event of such a group (smallest zone start, then zone end, then enzyme name) is applied". compareCleavages() actually sorts by `a.lo, a.hi, a.top, a.enzyme, ...`, comparing `top` before the enzyme name.

For two events with the same cut zone but opposite overhang orientation, the 5′-overhang event (top = lo) therefore always wins, whatever the names. This happens for any neoschizomer pair in a double digest, e.g. ApaI GGGCC^C vs PspOMI G^GGCCC, or KpnI vs Acc65I. A user reading the documented rule to predict the ends of a double digest gets the wrong answer. The behaviour is the same on linear and circular molecules.

Fix either the comparator (enzyme name before `top`) or the documentation.
expected: Per the documented rule (same zone start and end, then enzyme name), ApaI is applied: fragments 'AAAGGGCCC' with a right 3′ overhang of 4 and 'GCCCAAA' with a left 3′ overhang of 4. PspOMI is reported as a conflict.
actual: PspOMI is applied: fragments 'AAAGGGCC' with a right 5′ overhang of 4 and 'GGCCCAAA' with a left 5′ overhang of 4. ApaI is reported in `skipped` as a conflict. The same happens on the circular molecule.

title: Identical breaks are merged before the sticky-end check, so a valid cut is silently lost (adding an enzyme can remove another enzyme's cut)
description:
`collectCleavages` (digest.ts lines 226-228) sorts all cleavage events and drops every event whose (top, bottom) equals the previous one. The kept event is the first by (lo, hi, top, enzyme name, siteStart, strand). This happens before `digestLinear` runs its per-event checks (lines 265-273). Those checks depend on the recognition site, not only on the break: `e.siteStart < dsStart || e.siteStart + e.siteSize > dsEnd`.

With sticky input ends, the kept duplicate's site can lie partly in the single-stranded overhang while the dropped duplicate's site is fully double-stranded. The kept event is then skipped with reason 'end', and the dropped one is never considered. The enzyme that should cut does not appear in `skipped` either. For a React UI the cut simply vanishes, with no explanation.

It is also non-monotonic: a BsmAI digest cuts, but a BsaI + BsmAI digest of the same molecule does not. This matters because BsmAI's site GTCTC lies inside every BsaI site (GGTCTC) and every BsmBI/Esp3I site (CGTCTC), always with the same break. It also happens with a single enzyme that has twin Type IIS sites making the same break (MlyI). Blunt-ended linear molecules and circles are not affected, because there the checks depend only on the cut zone.

Oracle: pydna 5.5.16 `Dseq.from_full_sequence_and_overhangs('GGTCTC'+'A'*24, -1, 0).cut(BsaI, BsmAI)` returns 2 fragments (get_cutsites → [((7, -4), BsmAI)]).

Suggested fix: check applicability for each event before merging duplicates, or merge only among applicable events, and report the merged enzymes.
expected: 2 fragments, [0,11) and [7,30), as pydna gives and as the BsmAI-only digest gives. The break at top 7 / bottom 11 is made by BsmAI, whose site is fully double-stranded. Likewise MlyI's reverse site at 16 cuts at 11.
actual: 1 fragment, the intact molecule [0,30). `skipped` contains only {enzyme:'BsaI', reason:'end', message:'BsaI (site at 1) cannot cut: its recognition site is not fully double-stranded'}. BsmAI is not mentioned anywhere. MlyI: 1 fragment, with skipped [{MlyI, site 1..6, reason 'end'}]; the reverse site at 16 is lost.

title: Conflict resolution depends on the strand the sequence is written on: pUC19 and its reverse complement give different digests
description:
`applyInOrder` (digest.ts line 232, rule in the file comment lines 13-21) walks 5'→3' along the top strand. It keeps the first event of each group of conflicting cut zones. If the same physical molecule is written as its reverse complement, the walk runs the other way, so a different event is kept. The implementation explicitly makes circular results independent of the origin, but not of the strand. The known limitations mention only the origin case.

Real data, pUC19 (fixture M77789):
- BsaJI alone (commercial, NEB; two overlapping CCNNGG sites at the SmaI site of the MCS, at 266 and 267, with conflicting zones [267,271] and [268,272]) gives [2078,425,136,63] versus [2078,425,137,62] for the reverse complement.
- AccII + BsmBI gives 10 fragments versus 11. In the forward reading, BsmBI's zone [677,681] is kept and both AccII blunt cuts at 679 and 681 are skipped. In the reverse reading, both AccII cuts are kept and BsmBI is skipped, which adds a 2 bp fragment and changes 104/46 to 100/44.

Scan of enzyme pairs on circular plasmids:

| Plasmid | Pairs with different fragment sizes (common × commercial) | Pairs with different fragment counts (all commercial pairs) |
|---|---|---|
| pUC19 | 1,134 | 42 |
| pBR322 | 747 | 8 |

Reverse-complementing a map is a routine editor action, and Addgene and GenBank maps often differ in orientation. Users will therefore see the virtual digest change, including fragment ends used for in-silico cloning.

When two mirror-image events conflict, no deterministic rule can keep exactly one of them without depending on orientation. Suggested fix: either make the choice independent of orientation where possible, or document the dependence and flag the affected events (for example a skip reason meaning 'ambiguous') so the UI can explain it.
expected: The same physical molecule gives the same fragments whichever strand it is written on: identical sizes and the same number of fragments. If that is impossible in a symmetric conflict, the dependence should be documented and the affected events flagged.

title: nonCutters(sites, enzymes) returns enzymes that are not in `enzymes`
description:
The TSDoc of `nonCutters` (sets.ts line 41) says: "Names of the enzymes of `enzymes` that do not cleave the molecule at all". The function delegates to `cuttersWithCount(sites, 0, enzymes)`, which starts from `countCuts(sites)`, and that holds every enzyme present in `sites`. Any enzyme in `sites` whose sites cannot be cleaved (sites near the ends of a linear molecule, cuts: []) is therefore returned even when it is not in `enzymes`.

A natural UI pattern triggers this: compute `sites` once for the enzymes on the map, then ask which enzymes of the user's selection do not cut. Type IIS sites near linear ends are common, so the answer gets polluted with unselected enzymes.
expected: ['EcoRI']: only enzymes of the given list.

title: digest accepts input ends that cover the whole molecule and returns a fragment with zero base pairs
description:
`checkEnds` (digest.ts line 164) rejects ends whose lengths sum to more than L, with the error 'Single-stranded ends (...) are longer than the molecule'. It accepts a sum of exactly L, which is the same physical impossibility: no base pair is left. With left 3' 4 and right 5' 4 on an 8-mer, the top strand is empty. `digest` then returns that "duplex" as a fragment, which breaks the module's own invariant of at least 1 bp of duplex per fragment (asserted in digest.test.ts `checkInvariants`). Downstream ligation or gel code would treat a single-stranded oligo, or two unpaired strands, as a double-stranded molecule.

This input can arise from a record whose `ends` came from a file, or after the user trims a sticky-ended fragment. The check should be `>=`, or `L - left - right < 1`.
expected: An explicit Error, the same as for ends longer than the molecule, because the ends leave no base pair.
actual: No error. It returns [{seq:'AAAATTTT', topology:'linear', ends:{left:{kind:'3prime',length:4}, right:{kind:'5prime',length:4}}, parentRange:{start:0,end:8}, length:8}], whose duplex is 8 - 4 - 4 = 0 bp.

title: Enzyme map and cut counts ignore sticky ends: they report cuts inside single-stranded overhangs that digest() refuses to make
description: Linear records with single-stranded ends are normal in this app. SeqRecord.ends exists in types.ts, the ops module keeps ends through edits, and every digest product has sticky ends. But findSites, findSitesForEnzyme and countCuts have no input for the ends, and neither do the sets helpers built on them (uniqueCutters, cuttersWithCount, nonCutters). They apply the blunt-end Biopython rule (both cuts in [1, L-1]), so a recognition site that lies in a single-stranded overhang is listed with a cleavage event. digest(seq, 'linear', enzymes, { ends }) correctly refuses that same event (reason 'end': the site is not double-stranded). The map and cutter lists therefore contradict the digest of the same record. Almost every common cloning end hits this, because its overhang contains a 4-cutter site: XhoI or SalI ends (TCGA) show TaqI; HindIII or SacI ends (AGCT) show AluI and CviKI-1; XbaI, SpeI or NheI ends (CTAG) show BfaI; NcoI or SphI ends (CATG) show CviAII; KpnI ends show RsaI and Csp6I; PstI ends show HpyCH4V; NotI ends show HaeIII. In the reproduction, a standard EcoRI-XhoI directional-cloning insert lists TaqI as a unique cutter, yet TaqI cannot cut it at all. The spec signature of findSites has no ends parameter, so this is a gap in the API rather than a deviation from the spec. However, the UI has no correct alternative and would have to re-implement digest's end rule. Suggested fix: add an optional ends argument (e.g. findSites(seq, topology, enzymes, { ends })) that applies digest's rule: the cut zone must leave at least 1 bp inside the duplex and the site must be fully double-stranded.
expected: For a sticky-ended linear record there is a search that agrees with digest(..., { ends }). The TaqI site in the single-stranded TCGA overhang is reported without a cleavage event (or omitted), so countCuts gives TaqI 0 and uniqueCutters does not list it.
actual: findSites returns [{enzyme:'TaqI', range:{start:93,end:97}, strand:1, cuts:[{top:94,bottom:96}]}] on the 97-nt fragment, whose last 4 bases exist only on the bottom strand. countCuts gives TaqI = 1 and uniqueCutters = ['TaqI']. digestDetailed with the fragment's ends makes 0 cuts and reports 'TaqI (site at 94) cannot cut: its cut (top 94, bottom 96) is not inside the double-stranded part of the molecule'.

title: digestSizes, documented 'for gel lanes', returns the same sizes for an uncut supercoiled plasmid and for a linear molecule
description: digestSizes is documented, in the spec and in digest.ts, as giving fragment lengths 'for gel lanes'. It drops DigestFragment.topology. When the enzymes do not cut a circular molecule, it returns [L], exactly what it returns for a linear molecule of length L. A lane built from these sizes would draw the uncut plasmid as a linear L-bp band, which is how a linearized plasmid looks. The gel module (gel/lane.ts GelFragment.form: 'linear' | 'supercoiled' | 'nicked') needs the conformation, and supercoiled DNA runs much faster. With digestSizes alone, a virtual gel cannot answer the classic diagnostic question 'did my enzyme linearize the plasmid?'. NotI (no site) gives [2006] and EcoRI (one site) gives [2010]: both are a single band at about 2 kb. digest() does carry topology, but the helper meant for gel lanes cannot express it.
expected: The gel-lane helper tells the caller that a circular molecule was not cut, so a lane can draw it as supercoiled. For example, it returns { size, form } entries, or the docs point gel code to digest() topology.
actual: digestSizes(plasmid, 'circular', [NotI]) and digestSizes(plasmid, 'linear', []) both return [2006]. digestSizes(plasmid, 'circular', [EcoRI]) returns [2010]. The uncut and the linearized lanes therefore look the same.

title: Digest results share objects: uncut circles return the frozen BLUNT singleton for both ends, and neighbouring fragments share one DigestCut object
description: The rules say functions return new objects. digestCircular returns `ends: { left: BLUNT, right: BLUNT }` for an uncut circle (digest.ts ~line 611). BLUNT is a module-level Object.freeze'd constant, so left === right and both are frozen. A consumer that adjusts an end in place (`frag.ends.left.length = 4`) gets a TypeError, but only in this one case: every other result has fresh, mutable ends. digestLinear and digestCircular also build one DigestCut per boundary, so fragment i's rightCut is the same object as fragment i+1's leftCut. For a circle cut once, leftCut === rightCut. A consumer that turns one fragment into a new record and shifts its coordinates in place silently corrupts the neighbouring fragment.
expected: Each fragment has its own non-frozen ends and cut objects, like every other digest result.
actual: For an uncut circle, ends.left === ends.right and both are frozen: mutating one throws 'TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'length''. Adjacent fragments share one DigestCut object: editing frags[1].leftCut.top from 3 to 0 also changed frags[0].rightCut to {top: 0, bottom: 7}.

title: findSites can emit negative zero (-0) as a circular cut position
description: siteCuts normalizes circular cut positions with the shared mod() helper. mod(n, L) returns -0 when n is a negative multiple of L, because -15 % 15 === -0 and the r < 0 test is false. So when footprint start + cut offset equals -L, the reported CutPair contains -0. This happens when the enzyme's reach is at least L: circles shorter than about 30 bp for catalogue enzymes such as BaeI, MmeI or Type IIS enzymes on the bottom strand, or user-defined enzymes with large upstream offsets (validateEnzyme accepts up to ±1000). -0 equals 0 under ===, but Object.is, Vitest toEqual, React's Object.is state comparisons and Number#toLocaleString / Intl.NumberFormat (which prints '-0') treat it differently. digest() is not affected, because its toCut only applies mod to non-negative values. The fix belongs in search.ts (e.g. `mod(x, L) + 0`), since range.ts is shared.
